text:
Madame de Clèves had indeed suspected that this prince had noticed the feeling she had shown for him, and his words made her see that she had not been mistaken. It caused her great pain to see that she was no longer mistress of concealing her feelings, and that she had allowed them to appear to the Chevalier de Guise. It also caused her much pain that Monsieur de Nemours should know them; but this latter pain was not so complete, and it was mingled with a certain sweetness.

The Dauphine, who was extremely impatient to know what was in the letter Châtelart had given her, approached Madame de Clèves:

“Go and read this letter,” she said to her; “it is addressed to Monsieur de Nemours and, to all appearances, it is from that mistress for whom he has forsaken all the others. If you cannot read it now, keep it; come to my coucher this evening to return it to me and to tell me whether you recognize the handwriting.”

The Dauphine left Madame de Clèves after these words, and left her so astonished and in such great consternation that for some time she was unable to leave the spot. Her impatience and agitation did not allow her to remain with the queen; she went home, although it was not the hour at which she was accustomed to retire. She held the letter in a trembling hand; her thoughts were so confused that she had no distinct one, and she found herself suffering a kind of unbearable pain which she did not know and had never felt before. As soon as she was in her private chamber, she opened the letter and found it to read as follows:

LETTER

“I have loved you too much to allow you to believe that the change you perceive in me is an effect of my inconstancy; I want you to know that your infidelity is its cause. You are greatly surprised that I speak to you of your infidelity; you had concealed it from me with such skill, and I took such care to conceal from you that I knew of it, that you have good reason to be astonished that it is known to me. I myself am surprised that I was able to keep any sign of it from appearing to you. No pain has ever equaled mine. I believed that you had a violent passion for me; I no longer concealed from you the passion I had for you, and at the very time when I allowed you to see it in its entirety, I learned that you were deceiving me, that you loved another, and that, to all appearances, you were sacrificing me to this new mistress. I learned it on the day of the ring-tilting tournament; that was why I did not go. I pretended to be ill in order to conceal the disorder of my mind; but I did in fact become ill, and my body could not withstand so violent an agitation. When I began to recover, I continued to pretend that I was very ill, so as to have a pretext for neither seeing you nor writing to you. I wanted time to decide how I should conduct myself toward you; twenty times I made and abandoned the same resolutions; but at last I found you unworthy of seeing my pain, and I resolved not to let it appear to you. I wanted to wound your pride by making you see that my passion was weakening of its own accord. I believed that in this way I would diminish the value of the sacrifice you were making of it; I did not want you to have the pleasure of showing how much I loved you in order to appear more lovable because of it. I resolved to write you cold and languishing letters, so as to plant in the mind of the woman to whom you gave them the thought that you were ceasing to be loved. I did not want her to have the pleasure of learning that I knew she was triumphing over me, nor to increase her triumph by my despair and my reproaches. I thought that I would not punish you enough by breaking with you, and that I would cause you only slight pain if I ceased to love you when you no longer loved me. I found that you had to love me in order to feel the pain of not being loved, which I was experiencing so cruelly. I believed that if anything could rekindle the feelings you had had for me, it was to make you see that mine had changed; but to make you see it while pretending to conceal it from you, and as though I had not had the strength to admit it to you. I settled upon this resolution; but how difficult it was for me to make, and how impossible it seemed to carry out when I saw you again! A hundred times I was on the point of bursting out with reproaches and tears; the state in which my health still left me helped me to disguise my agitation and affliction from you. I was then sustained by the pleasure of dissembling with you as you dissembled with me; nevertheless, I did myself such great violence in order to tell you and write to you that I loved you that you saw sooner than I had intended to let you see that my feelings had changed. You were wounded by it; you complained of it. I tried to reassure you; but it was in so forced a manner that you were even more thoroughly convinced that I no longer loved you. At last, I did everything I had intended to do. The capriciousness of your heart made you return to me as you saw me drawing away from you. I have enjoyed all the pleasure vengeance can give; it seemed to me that you loved me more than you had ever done, and I made you see that I no longer loved you. I had reason to believe that you had entirely abandoned the woman for whom you had forsaken me. I also had reasons to be convinced that you had never spoken to her of me; but your return and your discretion have not been able to make amends for your inconstancy. Your heart was divided between me and another; you deceived me; that is enough to deprive me of the pleasure of being loved by you as I believed I deserved to be, and to leave me in the resolution I have made never to see you again, and by which you are so surprised.

Madame de Clèves read this letter and reread it several times, without nevertheless knowing what she had read. She saw only that Monsieur de Nemours did not love her as she had thought, and that he loved other women whom he deceived as he did her. What a sight and what knowledge for a person of her disposition, who had a violent passion, who had just given signs of it to a man whom she judged unworthy of it, and to another whom she was treating badly for love of him! Never had affliction been so piercing and so acute: it seemed to her that what gave this affliction its bitterness was what had taken place that day, and that if Monsieur de Nemours had had no reason to believe that she loved him, she would not have cared that he had loved another woman. But she was deceiving herself; and this pain she found so unbearable was jealousy, with all the horrors that can accompany it. She saw from this letter that Monsieur de Nemours had long been engaged in a love affair. She found that the woman who had written the letter had wit and merit; she seemed to her worthy of being loved; she found in her more courage than she found in herself, and she envied the strength she had had to conceal her feelings from Monsieur de Nemours. She saw from the end of the letter that this person believed herself loved; she thought that the discretion this prince had shown her, and by which she had been so deeply touched, was perhaps only the effect of the passion he had for this other person, whom he feared to displease. In short, she thought of everything that could increase her affliction and her despair. How often did she turn her thoughts back upon herself! What reflections did she make upon the advice her mother had given her! How greatly she repented not having persisted in withdrawing from society despite Monsieur de Clèves, or not having followed the thought she had had of confessing to him the inclination she felt for Monsieur de Nemours! She found that she would have done better to reveal it to a husband whose goodness she knew, and who would have had an interest in concealing it, than to allow it to be seen by a man who was unworthy of it, who deceived her, who was perhaps sacrificing her, and who thought of being loved by her only out of pride and vanity. In short, she found that all the misfortunes that could befall her, and all the extremities to which she might be driven, were less than having allowed Monsieur de Nemours to see that she loved him and knowing that he loved another woman. All that consoled her was the thought that, at least after learning this, she no longer had anything to fear from herself and that she would be entirely cured of the inclination she had for this prince.
